title: The synagogue today
hookLine: synagogues of every size and style, from shtiebels to cathedrals

lines: A ROOM UP A NARROW STAIRCASE.
A GRID OF FACES ON A SCREEN.
cards: Up a narrow staircase, past a rack of coats, there's a room the size of a living room. A bookcase bursting with worn volumes. A small cabinet against one wall.
Folding chairs that don't match. Men and women drift in on a weekday morning, nodding hello. Across town stands a building with a great dome, tall windows and seats for a crowd.
And somewhere else, a laptop is open on a kitchen table, a grid of faces waiting to begin. All three are synagogues.

teach.h: BEIT KNESSET: A HOUSE OF GATHERING.
teach.b: In Hebrew, a synagogue is a beit knesset, a house of gathering. That's the heart of it: not first a building, but people coming together.
The Torah sets the pattern when God tells Moses: "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." Some readers linger on the last words: not dwell in it, but among them.

teach.h: A LITTLE SANCTUARY IN EVERY LAND.
teach.b: Later the prophet Ezekiel tells the exiles that God will be to the scattered people "as a little sanctuary", and the Talmud reads that as the synagogues and houses of study wherever Jews live. So what makes one? Not size.

teach.h: TEN PEOPLE, AND NO RABBI REQUIRED.
teach.b: The Mishnah says certain parts of the service, like reading the Torah aloud to the congregation, need ten people, a minyan. Nothing there requires a rabbi; a knowledgeable member can lead the prayers.
Inside there's usually an ark holding the Torah scrolls, a lamp kept burning that recalls the lamp in the ancient sanctuary, and a reading table. Synagogues are traditionally built to face Jerusalem.

Then the styles spread out: a Hasidic shtiebel, a small room used as a synagogue, full of books, study and prayer; a grand domed building with a choir; a Sephardi synagogue with the reading table in the middle and seats around it.
Orthodox synagogues seat men and women separately; Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist synagogues usually seat families together. Some communities meet in a rented hall, a home or online.
Each is a house of gathering in its own way.

how: Jews gather in synagogues of every size for prayer, Torah reading, study, celebrations and mourning; some prayers need a minyan of ten, services can be led by any knowledgeable member, and some congregations also stream services online.

games.q: you're one of nine people in a small shtiebel on a weekday morning, ready to read from the Torah. what do you do?
o: read from the Torah anyway; nine is close enough.
wait, or go out and find a tenth person.
games.why: the Mishnah says reading the Torah to the congregation needs ten. communities wait, or go knocking, for the tenth.

practice: Think of a room where people you care about come together, a kitchen, a team, a place of worship, and what makes it a gathering place: the faces, the sounds, the greetings at the door.

Then picture a synagogue near you, or one that streams its services, and yourself stepping in as a guest who simply wants to see. If you pray, you can pray in your own words for the people who gather there.

wordCard.voice: Beit knesset. Hebrew for a house of gathering: the everyday word for a synagogue, whether a small shtiebel, a domed hall, or a screen of faces. Today's word.
